content.intro: This lesson introduces understanding rebasing as part of Rebasing and History Management. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: Rebase reapplies commits onto a new base and can create replacement commit IDs. It can make a private feature branch easier to review but should not casually rewrite public/shared history.

content_blocks.title: Merge and rebase compare
content_blocks.alt_text: Merge joins histories, often with a merge commit. Rebase replays commits onto a new base and changes the identities of replayed commits.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Rebase reapplies commits onto a new base and can create replacement commit IDs. It can make a private feature branch easier to review but should not casually rewrite public/shared history.

For **Understanding Rebasing**, keep the named subtopics in view: Reapplying commits onto a different base; How rebasing changes commit identities; Rebase versus merge; When rebasing is appropriate. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Rebase replays commits onto a new base and can change commit IDs. Use a private disposable feature branch first, then compare history before and after.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
